stages.title: Recognise the family
stages.description: Start with account names. Identify what each one represents before thinking about Dr or Cr.

questions.q: Money held in the business bank account is normally in which family (assuming no overdraft)?
questions.hint: The business controls this resource.
questions.explain: Bank funds are an asset. An overdraft would instead be a liability: always read the context.

questions.q: Trade payables records amounts the business owes to suppliers. Which family?
questions.hint: Payable means owed BY the business.
questions.explain: Trade payables is a liability: suppliers have provided goods or services and are waiting for payment.

questions.q: Sales records goods supplied to customers. Which family?
questions.hint: This account records what was earned, not what the customer still owes.
questions.explain: Sales is revenue. Bank or Trade receivables is the other account, depending on when the customer pays.

questions.q: The owner contributes personal savings to the business. The Capital account belongs to which family?
questions.hint: Owner funding is not a sale or a bank loan.
questions.explain: Capital is equity contributed by the owner. It is not revenue earned from customers.

questions.q: Electricity expense represents power used by the business this year. Which family?
questions.hint: The account records a benefit already consumed.
questions.explain: Electricity expense is an expense even if the bill has not yet been paid. An unpaid obligation is recorded separately.

questions.q: Loan receivable records a loan the business made to someone else. Which family?
questions.hint: The business is the lender. Money is owed TO it.
questions.explain: Loan receivable is an asset: a right to recover principal. Loan payable would mean the business borrowed.

stages.title: Translate the wording
stages.description: Pick one specific account from a short story. Look for who owes whom and whether a benefit has been used.

questions.q: Goods were supplied today, but the customer will pay next month. Which account records what the customer owes?
questions.hint: A credit customer owes money TO us.
questions.explain: Trade receivables is the asset recording the customer's debt. Sales records the revenue, not the outstanding amount.

questions.q: Insurance was paid for in full. At year-end, some cover relates to next year. Which account holds the unused benefit?
questions.hint: We paid before using the benefit; we are not the insurer receiving a customer's advance.
questions.explain: Prepayments is an asset for paid-for cover still to be used. Only cover used this year stays in Insurance expense.

questions.q: December electricity has been used but not billed, paid or recorded. Which account records the missing obligation?
questions.hint: A cost has been incurred and we still owe payment.
questions.explain: Accruals is the liability for the missing expense. Accrued income would be money earned by us, an asset.

questions.q: A customer pays now for a service the business will provide next year. Which account records the service still owed?
questions.hint: We received money, but have not earned it yet.
questions.explain: Income received in advance is a liability: we owe performance. It is not the same as a prepaid expense.

questions.q: A sole trader takes business funds for personal shopping. Which account records the withdrawal?
questions.hint: The owner is taking resources for personal use, not earning wages in this example.
questions.explain: Drawings reduces equity. Personal spending is not a business expense and does not belong in Purchases.

questions.q: The business buys a computer to use for several years, not to resell. Which account records its original cost?
questions.hint: Buying for long-term use is different from buying resale goods.
questions.explain: Equipment cost is a non-current asset. Depreciation expense allocates its depreciable cost over time; Purchases is for resale goods in this site's periodic system.

stages.title: Find both accounts
stages.description: Read the whole transaction and identify the two sides. Keep payments separate from the original sale or cost.

questions.q: At year-end, £275 of electricity has been used but not billed, paid or recorded. Which journal is needed?
questions.hint: Used = expense. Still owed and unrecorded = liability. No cash moves now.
questions.explain: Dr Electricity expense recognises this year's cost; Cr Accruals recognises the obligation. Bank is unchanged because no payment occurred.

questions.q: Pay £420 from bank towards a supplier invoice already recorded last month. Which journal?
questions.hint: Do not record the purchase again. Clear the recorded liability.
questions.explain: Trade payables decreases with a debit; Bank decreases with a credit. The purchase or expense was recorded with the invoice.

questions.q: A customer pays £360 for a credit sale already recorded. Which journal?
questions.hint: Swap 'customer owes us' for 'money in bank'.
questions.explain: Debit Bank and credit Trade receivables. The cash receipt clears an asset; it is not another sale.

questions.q: Insurance expense includes £900 that relates entirely to next year. Which year-end adjustment?
questions.hint: Move the unused part out of expense into an asset; no new payment occurs.
questions.explain: Dr Prepayments creates the future-benefit asset. Cr Insurance expense removes next year's cost from this year's expense.

questions.q: Pay a £100 covered warranty claim from bank. The expected cost was already provided for. Which journal?
questions.hint: The expense was recognised when the provision was created. Use that liability now.
questions.explain: Debit Warranty provision to reduce the existing liability; credit Bank. Charging Warranty expense again would double-count the covered cost.

questions.q: £200 service income has been earned but not received or recorded. Which journal?
options: Dr Accrued income £200; Cr Service income £200
Dr Prepayments £200; Cr Income received in advance £200
questions.hint: We have earned income and have a right to collect, but no cash yet.
questions.explain: Accrued income is an asset, increased by a debit. Service income is earned income, increased by a credit. This is not an expense accrual.

stages.title: Reason through the tricky cases
stages.description: Distinguish close matches, split transactions and check the meaning behind a normal balance.

questions.q: A £220 loan repayment comprises £200 principal and £20 interest. Which accounts and amounts are correct?
options: Dr Loan receivable £200; Dr Interest income £20; Cr Bank £220
Dr Loan payable £200; Dr Interest expense £20; Cr Bank £220
questions.hint: Principal clears a liability; interest is a cost; bank records all the cash.
questions.explain: The £200 debit reduces Loan payable, the £20 debit records Interest expense and the £220 credit reduces Bank. Neither the whole payment nor its principal is an expense.

questions.q: Accumulated depreciation normally has a credit balance. Why is it grouped with assets in the reference?
options: It is a contra-asset reducing carrying amount, not a liability
Every credit balance is an asset
It is cash saved to replace equipment
It records this year's depreciation expense only
questions.hint: Category follows what an account represents, not just its Dr/Cr balance.
questions.explain: Accumulated depreciation offsets asset cost. Depreciation expense records the current charge. A credit balance alone does not mean an account is a liability.

questions.q: The business receives a £50 dividend on shares it holds in another company. Which is correct?
questions.hint: We are the investor RECEIVING a return, not distributing money to our owners.
questions.explain: Dividend income is income earned on an investment. Dividends paid by this business to its own owners would be an equity distribution, not an expense.

questions.q: An asset cost £4,000, accumulated depreciation is £2,600 and proceeds are £1,200. After posting these to Disposal, where does the remaining result go?
questions.hint: Carrying amount = cost less accumulated depreciation. Compare proceeds with that amount.
questions.explain: Carrying amount is £1,400 and proceeds £1,200, so the loss is £200. Dr Loss on disposal £200; Cr Disposal £200 clears the temporary account.

questions.q: A previously deferred £9,000 grant covers three equal years of qualifying costs. Conditions are met. Which entry releases one year's income?
options: Dr Grants paid expense £3,000; Cr Bank £3,000
Dr Grant income £3,000; Cr Deferred grant income £3,000
Dr Deferred grant income £3,000; Cr Grant income £3,000
questions.hint: Reduce the deferred liability and recognise income; the cash arrived earlier.
questions.explain: Under the stated deferral model, £9,000 ÷ 3 = £3,000. Debit Deferred grant income and credit Grant income. There is no new cash receipt.

questions.q: Electricity £275 is used but unrecorded and unpaid. Separately, £120 of insurance already expensed is unused next-year cover. What do the adjustments create?
options: Accruals liability £275 and Prepayments asset £120; net profit falls £155
Accrued income asset £275 and Income in advance liability £120; profit rises £155
Two expenses totalling £395, with no asset or liability
questions.hint: Unpaid cost adds expense; unused paid cover removes expense. Neither adjustment moves cash.
questions.explain: Electricity: Dr expense £275, Cr Accruals £275. Insurance: Dr Prepayments £120, Cr expense £120. Net additional expense £155 reduces profit; both an asset and a liability arise.
